articles.title: Asians in Football: Frank Soo and the footballers that followed the Stoke City and England legend
articles.summary: The history of Asians in English football spans more than 125 years; England legend Frank Soo is among those that have blazed a trail for others to follow and was posthumously inducted into the National Football Museum Hall of Fame during Stoke City's Championship clash with Derby County
articles.body:
That England debut came in a wartime international in 1942, making Soo the first person of colour to play for the Three Lions - Plymouth Argyle trailblazer Jack Leslie, who was Black, was famously denied the opportunity to do so 17 years earlier because of the colour of his skin, despite earning an England call-up.

Soo made nine England appearances during the Second World War, but wartime games were not recognised as official matches by the Football Association. Soo and others who only played during the war never received an international cap. While the Leslie family received an honorary cap at Wembley Stadium last year, the Soo family are still waiting for his honorary England cap to this day.

Soo, who had an English mother and Chinese father, was snapped up as a teenager by Stoke City in 1933 from Liverpool-based Prescot Cables. His talent was identified by the same person who spotted Sir Stanley Matthews - a man regarded by many as one of the greatest players of his generation.

"The reports from his contemporaries were saying how good he (Soo) was," Lau says.

"He was the captain at Stoke, he captained Sir Stanley Matthews, he was the captain at Leicester (later in his career) and he also captained the RAF team.

"We talk about Sir Stanley Matthews, and he was the player and probably the gold standard back then. Frank was his contemporary, Frank was his captain - he should be spoken in the same words as him."

Former Eastern Eye sports editor Zohaib Rashid added: "He had the Three Lions on his chest, he represented England during some of the toughest years for the country [and] he was called up during the wartime and for victory matches. You can't ask for a higher honour than that."

Matthews and Soo also played together at national level during the Second World War, with some pointing to the discrimination suffered by Leslie as the reason why Soo never got an England call-up either side of the war.

"He represented his country [in every sense] during the Second World War. He was in the Royal Air Force," Soo's great niece Jacqui Soo explains.

"There was a cartoon in which he was portrayed as a Chinese figure and it said why is this person playing football for England and representing the national side - I think that had a detrimental effect on his football career."

Asians in the Premier League | Nev: Park was class

Against all odds, a number of Asian-heritage players have followed in Soo's footsteps, overcoming adversity to get on to the pitch in English football.

Sky Sports pundit Gary Neville played with one of the best Asian international footballers ever to grace the top division of the English game.

Former Manchester United and South Korea international Ji-Sung Park is one of just 47 Asian internationals to have played in the Premier League.

"Having an Asian in Ji-Sung Park playing for such a big club, it had a big impact on British football. It had a big impact in Korea as well and in Asian football," Neville says.

"Ji-Sung Park was a great team-mate, on the pitch and off the pitch and a dream of a person off the pitch in respect of his professionalism. He was very quiet, very humble, someone who was popular in the dressing room with all the players. He had a smile on his face, but very serious about his work.

"He was one of those players that you would put at the very top of the most underrated players that you would ever have played with at Manchester United.

"If we had a real problem defensively in a full-back area. Ji-Sung Park would play on that side and would double up with his full-back. He would do the donkey work, the hard work that basically is needed to be done to win a football match, which is not always the beautiful game.

"It's making sure that you protect and stop, and hassle and harass. And that's what he did - he pressed. We talk a lot about pressing a lot now - Ji-Sung Park did nothing but press. If Manchester United gave the ball away, he was always the first to react in a transition. We think of these as being new words, but he was doing that back then.

"He famously marked Andrea Pirlo, man-to-man in the San Siro. He doubled up on Lionel Messi in the Nou Camp. He played big roles for us defensively, but also was very important going forward."

Park changed perceptions in the English game just like Soo did decades earlier.

Tottenham head coach Ange Postecoglou has plenty of experience of working with East Asian talent, having managed in Japan where he guided Yokohama F Marinos to their first J League title in 15 years.

Postecoglou signed eight players of East Asian heritage during his two-year spell at Celtic prior to joining Spurs, including Reo Hatate, Daizen Maeda and Kyogo Furuhashi, who are now part of the backbone of Brendan Rodgers' side.

"I love the football, I really felt it was a real fertile ground," Postecoglou said.

"The first thing I did when I moved to Europe was to sign players from there, because I could see that unbelievable potential whether that be Japan or Korea. In that part of the world, they are really passionate about their football."

Postecoglou now manages South Korea superstar Heung-Min Son, who is the only Asian to score more than 100 goals in the Premier League.

But less than one per cent of players in the history of the Premier League have been Asian internationals - less than any other continent - with the highest number coming from Europe (79 per cent), according to figures provided by the Premier League towards the end of last season.

Today, the presence of Asians in football extends further, with visible representation now in disability football and at different levels of the women's game.

Sikh-Punjabi attacker Kira Rai was part of the Derby County side that made history by lifting the National Plate last season, and is one of the women breaking down barriers for British South Asians in football.

"People out there playing sports across the country of a South Asian heritage were not really given the platform to become visible," she says.

"Now they can see people that have paved the way and can think 'okay, if they can do it, I can do it'."

Azeem Amir became England's youngest-ever B1 blind footballer at the time of his international debut for the Three Lions in 2018.

"If I'm able to do something that people can only dream about and play for my country [I'm happy and proud], he says.

"By breaking the mould and becoming an elite-level sportsperson - if somebody is able to see that they can think I can be that person. And if we can create a cultural shift within society, I can say I did more than just play, I made a difference."

Former Liverpool and Arsenal winger Jimmy Carter was one of the first British South Asians to play in the Premier League. But his Asian heritage - through his father Maurice who hailed from the city of Lucknow in India - has only become more widely known in the last decade.

"Back in the day, and we are talking about over 30 years ago, there might have been an opinion that football is not for Asians," Carter says.

"For me to have represented two of the biggest clubs in world football in Arsenal and Liverpool was beyond my wildest dreams as a little kid, but back then, obviously, no-one really knew that I had Asian heritage.

"To some degree, I regret not giving that more of a voice [in order to inspire the next generation]."

Rashid added: "If you can't talk openly about some of the barriers that exist then we're not going to get the change that we want. There is so much talk in the current day about 'you can't be what you can't see'.

"The numbers might be small, but they've all got a story and they all have the potential to inspire someone.

"We need to know what it was that was their strength. Because from that, we can build strength in us."

For more stories, features and videos, visit our ground-breaking South Asians in Football page on skysports.com and stay tuned to Sky Sports News andour Sky Sports digital platforms.

articles.title: Morecambe latest news: Ashvir Singh Johal named new Shrimps manager
articles.summary: Ashvir Singh Johal has been named the new manager of Morecambe; He becomes the first Sikh to take charge of a professional British club after replacing sacked Derek Adams
articles.body:
The 30-year-old replaced Derek Adams, who was sacked on Monday, just a day after new owners Punjab Warriors completed the takeover which saved the club from extinction.

Sky Sports News understands new Morecambe owners Panjab Warriors had intended to appoint him in the summer but were delayed by the protracted sale of the club from Jason Whittingham's Bond Group.

A Morecambe statement said: "Ashvir Singh Johal arrives at the Mazuma Mobile Stadium with an excellent reputation as a forward-thinking coach and leader, bringing with him a wealth of experience in player development, tactical innovation, and building high-performance cultures.

"His appointment marks an exciting new era for the Shrimps as the club continues its journey under fresh ownership and renewed ambition."

Singh Johal worked closely with Kolo Toure when the pair were coaching under Brendan Rodgers at Leicester City. He went on to join the former Ivory Coast international at Wigan as first-team coach when Toure was appointed as the club's manager almost three years ago.

Sky Sports News exclusively revealed that the move to Wigan had made Singh Johal the first Sikh to take up a frontline coaching role in Sky Bet Championship history.

Singh Johal, who holds a UEFA Pro Licence, later had a spell as assistant coach to Cesc Fabregas at Como's academy in Italy and he now has a hefty in-tray at Morecambe, starting with building a squad as he currently only has five players under contract.

Morecambe, who were relegated from Sky Bet League Two last season, have had their first two National League games postponed after being suspended for failing to comply with the league's rules.

Singh Johal is due to be in the dugout as Morecambe are scheduled to open their campaign against Altrincham, though that game could also be in doubt given the club's current lack of players.

Despite the uncertainty of the immediate future, the new boss is looking to the long term.

"The immediate priority right now is going to be to identify the players that we need in this building to ensure Morecambe Football Club can perform well in the National League," he said in an interview with the club's official website.

"I think the short-term plan this year is to make sure that we retain our place in the National League by playing exciting, energetic football and working hard. I think that is a short-term aim.

"The long-term aim is to build the processes, the infrastructure. There's a clear commitment from the owners about the direction they want the club to go in.

"OK, now it's about building, and it's about growing and making sure that in three, four, five years' time, this is a completely energised and galvanised more football club that thrives in the EFL."

At 30, Singh Johal, who never played professional football and worked his way up the coaching ranks with a 10-year stint at Leicester, is one of the youngest coaches to earn the UEFA Pro Licence. He left Notts County in the summer where he was their B Team head coach.

On becoming a first-team manager for the first time, he added: "It's what I've wanted to do. It's been my dream since I was 14 or 15 years old.

"It's every single day that's been the target I've worked towards. But for me, now there's a new target, and the target is to make sure Morecambe is successful as a club.

"Make sure this year we don't just survive in the National League, we thrive."

Anti-discrimination charity Kick It Out applauded Singh Johal's appointment.

It said in a post on X: "History made. Congratulations to Ashvir Singh Johal on becoming the first Sikh manager in professional football.

"Fully deserved and also a significant milestone for representation in leadership within the game."

articles.title: Middle East crisis: Will Iran play at World Cup co-hosted by USA? How conflict affects sport
articles.summary: US and Israel hit targets across Iran on Sunday as part of an intensifying military campaign, which followed the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei; thousands of flights have been cancelled amid a crisis in the Middle East, which raises questions about how sport is affected
articles.body:
Iran's participation at the 2026 World Cup has been called into question after United States - co-hosts - and Israel launched air strikes at the country over the weekend, as Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed. The conflict has spread, with Iran launching attacks against US allies and assets in the Middle East.

The Iran football federation president, Mehdi Taj, told local state media that "we cannot be expected to look forward to the World Cup with hope." He added that "sports chiefs" would make a final decision on whether they could play or not.

Speaking with Sky News' Rob Harris , FIFA president Gianni Infantino said: " I hope so much, it will be a moment of peace. I hope we can contribute to unite the world a little bit. The world really needs it."

However, President Donald Trump said he didn't care with Iran competed or not, telling American outlet Politico : "I really don't care. I think Iran is a very badly defeated country. They're running on fumes."

General secretary of FIFA Mattias Grafstrom also said: "It's premature to comment on it in detail, but of course we will monitor the developments around all issues around the world, and I think we had the final draw in Washington where all teams participated, and of course our focus is to have a safe World Cup with everybody participating."

Sky Sports News contacted FIFA on Monday (February 3) and understands FIFA's stance has not changed in the last 48 hours.

So if Iran pull out of the World Cup, what options do FIFA have?

World football's governing body does have the authority to call in a replacement, should Iran not take part. Or they could make a slight change to the tournament make-up.

Article 6 of FIFA's 2026 World Cup regulations focuses on cases of non-participation. Regulation 6.5 relates to "force majeure", which is an unforeseen event. "If a Participating Member Association withdraws or a match cannot be played or is abandoned as a result of force majeure, the authorised FIFA organising body (including the Tournament Operation Centre) shall decide on the matter at its sole discretion and take whatever action is deemed necessary."

Regulation 6.7 then states: "If any Participating Member Association withdraws and/or is excluded from the FIFA World Cup 26, FIFA shall decide on the matter at its sole discretion and take whatever action is deemed necessary. FIFA may decide to replace the Participating Member Association in question with another association."

Sky Sports News' Chief Correspondent Kaveh Solhekol said on the matter: "FIFA has contingency plans in case Iran are not in the World Cup. It is at their discretion who would replace them, most likely Iraq or the United Arab Emirates."

In summary, FIFA has two options if Iran do not, or cannot play: draft in a replacement nation, or alter the rules of the competition so Iran's group would be a three-team section.

Iran have been drawn in Group G along with New Zealand, Belgium and Egypt.

Iran qualified automatically for the World Cup, with the United Arab Emirates losing out on an automatic qualification spot and subsequently going out in the play-off rounds. In the event of Iran not playing in the tournament, they would be the closest replacement.

Iraq could only be an option if they do not come through their intercontinental play-off against either Bolivia or Suriname in Mexico later this month. But under the rules, FIFA could decide to select a team from any association, not just the Asian Football Confederation, from where Iran qualified.

FIFA has yet to confirm a decision on whether or not the Finalissima game between European champions Spain and South American champions Argentina will go ahead in Qatar on March 27. Lionel Messi could lift another trophy but Qatar has suspended all football matches until further notice.

Cristiano Ronaldo's team, Saudi club Al Nassr, has already been affected by a wave of cancellations of Asian Champions League games, though the Saudi Pro League is continuing as it stands.

Meanwhile, Iran's women's football team opted not to sing the country's national anthem when they lined up against South Korea in the Asian Cup in Australia on Monday.

Crystal Palace and Liverpool 's away ties in Cyprus and Turkey are currently due to be played as scheduled, though UEFA has told Sky Sports News it is "closely monitoring" the situation.

Liverpool visit Galatasaray on March 10 for the first leg of the Champions League last 16 and Palace have been drawn against AEK Larnaca in the Europa Conference League, with the away tie on March 19.

Formula 1 - season-opener set to go ahead

Formula 1 is "closely monitoring" the ongoing conflict in the Middle East with races upcoming in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia next month.

No impact is expected for the season-opening Australian Grand Prix this weekend, although some flights for personnel have been rearranged as people planned to changeover in the Middle East on the way to Melbourne.

Roughly 2,000 people work at every F1 race, and it is thought at least a quarter had been due to travel to Australia via travel hubs such as Doha and Dubai.

China, Thailand, Korea, Japan, America, Singapore and Hong Kong have instead been used as stopovers by those scrambling to make it to Australia.

The Bahrain Grand Prix is scheduled to take place on April 10-12 with the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix on April 17-19.

"Our next three races are in Australia, China and Japan and not in the Middle East - those races are not for a number of weeks," said an F1 spokesperson.

"As always, we closely monitor any situation like this and work closely with relevant authorities."

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem added: "Safety and wellbeing will guide our decisions as we assess the forthcoming events scheduled there [in the Middle East]."

Meanwhile, the FIA has postponed the opening race of the World Endurance Championship which was originally scheduled to take place in Qatar at the end of March, moving the season's start to Italy in April.

The ECB released a statement on Saturday to announce it was following advice from the government, while confirming the cancellation of Sunday's 50-over game between the Men's Lions and Pakistan Shaheens in Abu Dhabi.

On Monday, they confirmed the remainder of the Lions' tour, as well as England Women's proposed trip to Abu Dhabi for a T20 Women's World Cup camp, would not go ahead - and the squad landed safely back in the UK on Tuesday.

"We are grateful to all those who provided assistance and advice while the squad were in Abu Dhabi, and who helped ensure their safe return," the ECB said in a statement.

"Our thoughts are with all those currently still in the Gulf who are seeking to return to the UK, and we hope they are able to get home soon."

England's men are currently competing in the T20 World Cup, where the semi-finals are being held in India.

The players are set to travel to Mumbai as planned for Thursday's semi-final, though the ECB insists "the safety and security of our teams and staff is our top priority. We are in contact with security experts and the Government in relation to current events in the Middle East, and are following official advice."

The West Indies and Zimbabwe teams have delayed their return from India after their ‌exit from the tournament due to international ​airspace closures.

England's Jonny Bairstow revealed on social media he remains in Dubai with his family having written to airline Emirates at the weekend regarding a cancelled flight.

"For those writing that I'm with the England Lions team, I am not," Bairstow wrote on X.

"I am with my young family in Dubai. Sure the England Lions security staff will be doing all they can to get them out of Abu Dhabi, but I am trying to keep my family safe and get us out of here."

Daniil Medvedev is among the tennis players and team members to have seen travel plans disrupted as he tries to leave Dubai.

The former US Open champion has just won the Dubai Tennis Championships after scheduled opponent Tallon Griekspoor was forced to withdraw ahead of the final due to injury.

Medvedev is due to compete at the BNP Paribas Open at Indian Wells in California, with main-draw matches due to begin on Wednesday.

His Instagram reposted a report from Russian-language tennis outlet Bolshe on Monday confirming his safety after flights were cancelled.

"The health, safety and wellbeing of our players, staff and tournament personnel is our priority. We can confirm that a small number of players and team members remain in Dubai following the conclusion of the recent ATP 500 event," the ATP Tour said in a statement Monday.

"They and their teams are being accommodated in the tournament's official hotels, where their immediate needs are being fully supported."

In the United Arab Emirates players were forced to evacuate the court at an ATP Challenger event after a drone attack on a nearby oil terminal.

The ATP subsequently cancelled the tournament on Tuesday amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle ‌East.

"Following ongoing security concerns in the ​region, the ATP Challenger Tour events scheduled in Fujairah this week and next week (Fujairah 2) have been cancelled," the ATP said in ​a statement.

"The safety and wellbeing of our players and ⁠tournament personnel is our highest priority. ⁠Players remain on site and are being fully supported, with accommodation and all immediate needs covered while ‌onward travel arrangements are explored."

Winter Paralympics - athletes facing travel issues

The International Paralympic Committee said some athletes are facing issues travelling to Milan-Cortina ahead of the Games beginning on Friday.

"We are in close contact with all delegations competing at the Games as well as other stakeholders. Many of the teams are already in Europe attending training or holding camps, but the closure of airspace in the Middle East is impacting the arrival of some stakeholders," the IPC said in a statement.

"We would prefer not to comment on the status of individual delegations or stakeholders at this stage but can provide assurance that we are working diligently with Milano Cortina 2026 to find solutions for those affected."

In horse racing, the Super Saturday meeting went ahead at Meydan, but Sunday brought further challenges as British racing personnel, including trainers and jockeys, found themselves stranded in Dubai.

Trainer Jamie Osborne was among many awaiting news of when they may be able to return to the UK, with flights suspended from Dubai International Airport.

He said: "It's annoying as I'd like to be back at home dealing with everything I should be dealing with at home, but we're stuck here and quite how we get home and when we get home is very much up in the air."

Super Saturday may have gone ahead as planned, but the Emirates Racing Authority postponed Sunday's card at Jebel Ali until March 15, with the course next set to stage racing next Sunday. Meydan is also slated to race a day earlier on March 7.

Elsewhere in the region, Bahrain is set to host the two-day King's Cup fixture on Thursday and Friday.

articles.title: Jess Thirlby steps down as England Netball head coach ahead of Commonwealth Games
articles.summary: Anna Stembridge will take over as England head coach for the 2026 Commonwealth Games following the departure of Jess Thirlby, who has stepped down after nearly seven years in the job since replacing Tracey Neville.
articles.body:
Assistant coach Anna Stembridge will take over as head coach throughout the Games, which take place from July 25 until August 2, having previously served in the role from 2011-2015, during which time she led the team to gold at the World Netball Series in Liverpool 2011.

Thirlby, who succeeded Tracey Neville in the job in July 2019, explained in a statement that she is standing down in order to focus on supporting her family.

"It is with a heavy heart that I share my decision to step down from my role as head coach at England Netball, effective immediately," Thirlby said in a statement.

"It has been an incredible six and a half years and the greatest privilege to be the Roses' longest-serving head coach. I am immensely proud of what we have achieved together - particularly the historic World Cup silver medal we fought so hard for, which resulted in our joint-highest world ranking.

"The dedication, passion, and excellence this team has shown has been nothing short of inspirational. No matter how much we love what we do, we are all still human. This is not a decision I had ever thought I would have to make but I need to turn my attention onto supporting my incredible family.

"On reflection, I was mistaken to not prioritise and process the loss of my father at the time of his death, instead, and without regret, travelling with the team for the World Cup and the subsequent series in New Zealand. Everything I have done since has been to prioritise the England Roses and with this in mind, I feel that stepping down as head coach now is best for me and my family."

During her time in the job Thirlby guided England to a historic silver medal at the 2023 World Cup before also winning the 2025 Netball Nations Cup.

She previously coached Team Bath and Celtic Dragons having also represented England as a player.

"I want to thank Jess for her time as head coach and for the dedication and commitment she has shown to the programme and the wider game over the past six and a half years," said England Netball CEO Fran Connolly.

"During her tenure, the side reached a historic Netball World Cup final, secured multiple series victories, and recorded wins against every nation ranked in the world's top five.

"We are grateful for the leadership and professionalism Jess has shown throughout and for the significant contribution she has made to the continued growth and development of the Roses programme. We wish Jess and her family the very best for the future.

"We now look ahead to building on these strong foundations as the Vitality Roses enter the next phase of their journey."

Former Roses captain Olivia Murphy joins the England set-up as assistant coach on a secondment from Loughborough Sport, while former Australian Diamonds captain Sharni Layton continues as specialist coach joined by 2018 Commonwealth Games gold medallist Jo Harten.

England, champions at the 2018 Commonwealth Games, enter this year's Games seeking a return to medal contention after losing in the bronze medal match in 2022.

"Looking ahead to the Commonwealth Games, I am proud of the foundations we have built together," Thirlby added. "The systems, structures and culture of excellence we have developed have created a strong and resilient team, capable of competing with the best on the international stage.

"The work put in by the players and staff has been exceptional, and I know the group will approach the Games with commitment and belief. I feel confident that the team is in a good place and well prepared for the next phase of their journey.

"This will ensure that the incredible momentum we have built continues, and that the team has the best possible preparation for the Games."

Thirlby described her time as Roses head coach as the "most rewarding" period of her professional career.

articles.title: Sky Sports push notifications FAQ: How to receive the news alerts you want
articles.summary: The Sky Sports mobile app will keep you up to date with the latest news from your favourite sports - here's how to receive the alerts you want.
articles.body:
Choose from streaming the live action on your mobile or tablet, receiving breaking news straight to your device or being notified when highlights from your favourite sports are available to watch so you don't miss a moment while out and about.

And this season, you can also watch vertical clips of the best Premier League action in the Sky Sports app!

For the best app and vertical video experience, make sure you have the latest version downloaded onto your phone or tablet.

Once you have updated to the latest version of the app and signed in, you can enjoy all the latest available features for the new Premier League season including vertical video highlights and filter Sky Sports' notifications to suit your needs...

Q: I want to be notified when a big sports news story breaks, but I don't want to sign up to receive individual sports alerts. Can I do that?

A: Yes! On the app home page, tap on the 'Profile' icon in the bottom-right hand corner and then tap notifications. On the next page, simply tap on 'Breaking News' and we'll send you a notification when a big story emerges. This way, you'll be notified when a top story arrives - but you won't receive daily individual sports alerts.

Q: I'm a football fan, but I'm keen to know when a big sports story breaks. I want to get all the latest football news, but would like to know who has won the latest Formula 1 Grand Prix or the result of a big Box Office event, for example. Is that possible?

A: It is! If you're keen on getting dedicated news alerts from an individual sport but want to know when a big sports story breaks, make sure you tap on the sport you love along with 'Breaking News'. This way, you'll be notified of a big story without having to subscribe to another sport.

Q: I want to receive the latest football, tennis, rugby league, darts, golf and boxing news. Can I subscribe to more than one sport?

articles.title: Luke Littler: Wayne Mardle hails Premier League champion for opening up about struggles, says he has 'no weaknesses'
articles.summary: Luke Littler questioned future after tough times in Brighton and Manchester during Premier League season; world No 1 beat Luke Humphries 11-10 in gripping final to lift trophy for second time in three years; Wayne Mardle says Littler playing at "peak level" and can win in different ways
articles.body:
Littler secured the title for the second time in three years and then became emotional in his on-stage interview as he discussed under-performing in Brighton earlier in the season, a week after being involved in an argument with Gian van Veen in Manchester.

The 19-year-old was knocked out in the quarter-finals on both of those nights and revealed after his triumph in London that he was considering his future at that point after booing from the crowd.

Littler said: "I was sat at home saying to [girlfriend] Faith, 'I don't want to do it any more, just the crowd every week'. I said to her, 'I'm down bad'."

Speaking following Littler's win over Humphries in the 17th week of competition, Mardle said the champion's admission of his struggles was a "step forward".

'I have nothing but admiration for this teenager'

Mardle told Sky Sports : "There is more that goes on in a Premier League than just turning up week after week. It is a rollercoaster for every player, whether you are winning games or struggling.

"We know there are worse jobs but for a dart player this is an endurance test. This is the culmination of all that effort and it came out for Littler. He was inconsolable.

"No one is that strong they don't have doubts. He had doubts but came back. Owning up to that is a step forward for him. I have nothing but admiration for this teenager.

"We know how strong Littler is mentally but when you are feeling like you're public enemy number one, you can feel like you don't want to turn up. But he did turn up and this is the by-product of turning up.

"I love the family support he has. His mum and dad travel everywhere, as does Faith. That's so important.

"You are never on your own. I was fortunate that I never played this sport on my own as when you do it is a lonely place. I have seen people want to walk away.

"But Luke has one of the best support systems there is in darts. It is a family affair and he has a great team behind him.

"I also love the reaction [to winning the title]. We want to see more of that. We don't want to see someone win a trophy and be like 'oh, I've won another one, so what?' That is marvellous to see.

"Even though he has been so successful, it still means the world."

Littler began the year by retaining his World Championship title and went on win the Saudi Arabia Masters, Winmau World Masters, UK Open and Poland Darts Masters before getting his hands on the Premier League trophy for a second time.

Mardle added of the world No 1: "He has the belief, he knows he has the ability and somehow he finds it within to keep doing it.

"There is a point in everyone's career when they are at their peak. We don't know if this is the peak, we have no idea, but we know this is the peak level as Michael van Gerwen's peak, Phil Taylor's peak, was this kind of standard.

"It's good enough time and time again. When he can run riot, he is happy with that. When he has to fight back, he is happy with that. When it goes to a last-leg decider, he is happy with that.

"There are no weaknesses. Back-to-back world champion, then he wins the Masters, then the UK Open after being in trouble a few times. He was in trouble a few times in the Premier League and won.

"The kid is never beaten until you are shaking his hand and holding that trophy."

articles.title: England Netball head coach Anna Stembridge 'confident' about Vitality Roses squad ahead of Commonwealth Games challenge
articles.summary: Anna Stembridge believes the Vitality Roses squad contains the players to compete for gold at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow this summer; watch live coverage of the Netball Super League semi-finals on Saturday on Sky Sports Mix and Sky Sports' YouTube from 2.30pm
articles.body:
Stembridge took charge of England for the second time - she was initially coach from 2011 to 2015 when known as Anna Mayes - in March when Jess Thirlby stepped down from the role.

The 45-year-old saw England lose agonisingly by one goal to both New Zealand and Australia at the 2014 Commonwealth Games, but is hopeful they can overcome their old rivals this time despite the lack of experience in the squad.

She has been encouraged by the form of some of the younger England players, particularly London Pulse's Olivia Tchine.

Speaking to Sky Sports' Off The Court podcast, Stembridge said: "I'm really confident about this squad. We've got a really beautiful blend in terms of - yes there's not loads that have been to Commonwealth Games, we've only got three athletes - however, on the flip side, you've got that excitement, that vibrancy in terms of people that have never been to a Commonwealth Games and that type of energy is infectious.

"So let's not underestimate what that can do to a squad as well. And we've got brilliant tactical diversity in this group which has always been a huge strength or a real tool to our armoury as an England side.

"We've got some world-class individuals and they are just getting better and better. Like when we see them on the world stage - Olivia Tchine, wow! Around 18 months ago when we went out to Australia and New Zealand she'd been to a World Cup but it was very much like as a peripheral 12.

"Since then it gives me goosebumps, she has literally put her hands up and gone, 'I'm here, I'm owning this stage', so people like that we're seeing really develop their trade and really stamp their authority.

"Super excited to see the likes of her saying, 'I'm here and I'm about, dominating this circle' as one example of someone we can be really excited about."

Stembridge, who was previously an assistant coach to Thirlby, also explained how she has spent her time over the past few weeks after returning to the senior position.

"It is an honour and it's an absolute privilege," she said. "This type of role is the pinnacle of most coach's careers. In this period of change I was the right person for the role - in terms of providing consistency, clarity for the players and stability.

"We've got some brilliant foundation and it's important we do build on that. First and foremost I wanted to get out into the clubs, build those connections with the players, build connections with the club coaches - they play such an important part in supporting our players that I wanted to lead by action and get out there, spending time with them in their environment.

"Also make sure as a coaching team that we are doing the analysis. We want to provide clarity in terms of game plan. I want the players to feel really well connected - us as coaches and support staff - and then to have that confidence going into the Commonwealth Games."

articles.title: World Matchplay Darts: Luke Littler draws fresh Phil Taylor comparisons after historic record-breaking Blackpool victory
articles.summary: Luke Littler posted the highest tournament average in World Matchplay Darts history to successfully defend his title in Blackpool; Littler thrashed Gerwyn Price to continue his run of winning every PDC major title in 2026 and receive fresh praise
articles.body:
Littler capped off a historic week at Blackpool's Winter Gardens becoming the first player since Michael van Gerwen to successfully defend his title, continuing his record of winning every PDC major title in 2026 so far.

The book of darting superlatives is rapidly running out of pages to describe Littler's brilliance, with the teenager continuing to climb to generational heights in the sport and overtake many records held by childhood idol Taylor.

Littler had already defended titles at the World Championship and the UK Open, plus won the Winmau World Masters, Premier League and the World Cup of Darts, with the 19-year-old now chasing more success in the months and years ahead.

"I don't think anyone has ever won every major in the calendar year and that is what we are pushing for," Littler told Sky Sports . "The family, they are always backing me a million per cent and that is what drives me on.

"I would absolutely love to be the greatest dart player there ever has been. As I have always said, I have got to win 16 of these, 16 worlds, and then have a look at whatever else Phil Taylor did win.

"I have got plenty more years. When am I going to retire? Who knows. I have still got plenty more years left in the tank."

Littler smashed the highest tournament average, posting 111.04 across his five matches to beat Taylor's 2010 previous best of 106.31, plus broke his own record of most 180s at a World Matchplay.

"I am very happy with myself and the performances, not only in the final but the past eight days, every round," Littler added. "It is crazy to say that the 109 average was my worst average throughout the tournament!"

Why time is required in Taylor comparisons

Littler may have his hands back on the trophy named after Taylor, but he would need to win every World Matchplay until 2040 just to equal the all-time title tally of 'The Power'.

In 2007, six months after Luke Littler was born, Phil Taylor made a quarter-final exit at the World Matchplay - just the second time this century that 'The Power' had been beaten on the Winter Gardens stage.

Seven years later, the week after Littler left year two of primary school, Taylor had still not lost another match at the event and was closing out a seventh consecutive World Matchplay title.

Taylor won a record 38 consecutive matches during that title streak and lost just eight times in his 24-year career at the World Matchplay, with no player since coming remotely close to beating those extraordinary achievements.

The trophy comparisons may be a mismatch but the scoring differences between the two are certainly not, with Littler posting the second-highest tournament winning average in the sport's history and just 0.5 points behind Taylor's 2009 European Championship win - despite playing over double the legs Taylor did that week

"I can still get better," Littler insisted in his press conference. "I can obviously get a lot better. Through the matches I was up to a 120 average at one point. I didn't stick at it, but maybe in a few years' time I will stick at it and go up to that when the match is finished.

"At the minute, I'm playing some of the best stuff and I've just got to keep it there."

Littler was described by Price as "one in a million" and has taken plenty of plaudits from his peers for his run to another TV title, with his success more impressive given the growing depth at the top of sport.

"Luke's dominance over the last 12 months has been very Taylor-esque and that's why he's reached that figure (£3m in prize money), which is a huge figure and one that we've never had before," PDC chief executive Matt Porter told Sky Sports .

"I don't think the mentality of the opponents is the same (as Taylor's era). 20-odd years ago, players would see getting to the final as their championship.

"You wouldn't get that answer off Gerwyn Price, you wouldn't get it off Luke Humphries, Michael Van Gerwen, Steven Bunting, Nathan Aspinall, Jonny Clayton - those guys are not here to make up the numbers.

"Luke at the moment is almost unstoppable. Nobody's ever unstoppable, but with the way he's playing, someone's really going to have to up their game if they're going to beat him."

Further title defences at the Boyle Sports World Grand Prix (September 28-October 4) and Mr Vegas Grand Slam of Darts (November 14-22) are to come for Littler, who already holds a record-breaking advantage at the top of PDC rankings.

Littler will look to claim his elusive TV ranked title at the European Championship (October 22-25), while winning all three would leave him just requiring the Players Championship Finals (November 27-29) to complete a sweep of every major and big TV event in a calendar year.

Phil Taylor's impressive 2009 season didn't contain the Premier League title or the World Cup of Darts, which didn't launch until the following year, while Van Gerwen's 2016 dominance was also missing World Cup glory. Littler has the chance to surpass both with his campaign.

Littler has been skipping ProTour events during the season to leave qualification for the Players Championship Finals in doubt, although his latest win - and thoughts of claiming all the majors in the same - has changed his schedule plans over the coming months.

"Coming into the tournament I'd won every major so far so this is what I wanted to do," Littler explained. "I have been checking the Pro Tour rankings - whoever is in 64th (final qualification spot) just keeps going up and up!

"I know there is four (Players Championship events) in Leicester I have got to go to now. If I don't qualify I will get grilled and if I qualify I will get grilled anyway, so who knows what is going to happen."

Littler has already cemented himself as one of the darting greats in just over two and a half years as a professional. The thought of him getting even better in pursuit of more records is a terrifying - but exciting - prospect.

articles.title: Luke Littler: Target Darts explain the science behind World No 1's phenomenal success
articles.summary: "He's back-to-back world champion, what he could do in the sport is entirely up to him" - James Tattersall, CEO of Target Darts, says the world is Luke Littler's oyster; you can watch the BoyleSports World Grand Prix live on Sky Sports from Sept 28 to Oct 4 in Leicester
articles.body:
Littler has spearheaded darts' surge towards the mainstream since he broke on the scene with his debut run to the 2024 World Championship final as a 16-year-old.

Darts manufacturer Target Darts has supported the global superstar since the age of 12. In February 2024, the teenager signed a multi-year mega-deal reported to be worth up to £20 million - the most lucrative the sport has ever seen.

Littler possesses a generational talent when it comes to playing darts and Sky Sports pundit Wayne Mardle has said "he's probably the most natural naturally gifted player I've ever seen in my life".

Since the moment the Warrington-born star first held a dart, he's become a record-breaker and history-maker.

James Tattersall, CEO of Target Darts, says both the company and Littler are "aligned" in where they want to see the future of darts go.

Speaking at an event in which Target have set out a vision to inspire 100 million people to play darts by the end of the decade, he explained the process of how Littler sat down with chairman Garry Plummer, the design team, and engineers to build darts to perfect his game.

"I think some of the inspiration was drawn from Adrian Lewis' darts and the pixel grip, which is a unique grip that Target has and that worked its way into building up Luke's original G1," said Tattersall. "That was the barrel, but over the years Luke's tweaked it and challenged us to improve it. The point length has changed, the shaft and flight have changed to a K-Flex system before his first World Championships."

F-Flex is a one-piece flight and shaft innovation that screws into the back of the barrel.

Tattersall explained: "What it helps you do is when you're throwing darts together in such tight groupings like Luke does, the thing you want to avoid is that dart coming in and deflecting off the dart that's already in the board and the K-Flex helps reduce those deflections substantially.

"And longer points - it's like the balance of the dart and how it flies and how it lands through the air. I think another part of it is it keeps the barrel section of the dart further away from the treble and that creates more space in the board."

"His talent is all down to him," says Tattersall. "I think when you're talking about the equipment, we're talking about making Luke comfortable with all of that talent and giving him the right equipment that he's confident with to use and just to get those last few percentages, but Luke's an extraordinary player regardless."

With two world titles in three visits to Alexandra Palace, and 14 major titles to his name, Littler is well on his way to joining Phil Taylor as a legend of the sport.

The problem for his rivals is that he is still getting better after the Warrington star crushed Gerwyn Price 18-9 to retain his Betfred World Matchplay title in Blackpool on Sunday.

Littler was in imperious form as he set a new record for the final with an average of 111.53, lifting his average for the tournament as a whole to 111.04 to break Phil Taylor's previous high mark of 106.31.

The win keeps Littler on course for a clean sweep of trophies in 2026 having already won the World Championship, UK Open, Premier League and the Masters.

Littler's management have invested in sports psychologists, nutritionists, performance coaches, and biomechanics in order to get the most out of their talent, and the teenager has benefitted in every area to help support his game.

"Mentality is absolutely key. We want to protect the players. The stage is lonely up there, and darts is a gruelling sport," Tattersall said.

"It's a bit like a penalty shootout, but every single time you're throwing a dart. It's such a closed skill, and it's so repetitive. Your mindset's got to be really, really clear, and you get those big momentum swings, you think you're about to checkout the double, you miss by a millimetre, your opponent throws in a big 170 checkout, and that's a punch in the stomach. It's how do you recover from that for the next leg? That's sports psychology, and it's crucial in all sports. I don't know why it's a surprise that it should not be in darts."

'We want to learn about action - not create robots'

With biomechanics, the cameras observe how a player throws darts, with sports science data helping ways of working on the technique in order to improve.

Target have ideas but Tattersall insists implementing them will not turn the Luke Littlers of this world into robots.

"That's the last thing we want to do," he said. "What we want to do is discover and learn about the sport, and learn about that action, because why is it that there are different throwing techniques?

"If you look at something like golf, where you know suddenly you come along with the Vardon grip [or overlapping grip], and that becomes almost the only way to hold a golf club.

"I think the high jump has got that really famous example of how the sport, science, innovated, [Fosbury flop], you ended up with that kind of one technique point.

"I think there will always be different ways of throwing a dart, and there will be different ways of improving those different styles, and maybe that particular style is because you're tall, and maybe that particular style is because you've got longer arms, we don't know yet, but that's what we're going to find out, and then use that data accordingly."

Zoe Burton, Chief Transformation Officer at Target Darts, says Littler is already inspiring the next generation with his natural talent, although the company are slowly moving towards a performance technology system, which is currently being tested on a number of players.

"If you look at a young person and you think of their journey as they get into a sport, you need an inspiring player - that person who they look up to - and can almost aspire to be. Luke Littler provides that," said Buton.

"You need a natural talent, but that gets you so far. Then it's determination and I think psychology as well.

"What makes a star player become a great and world-class player is actually their ability to focus under pressure and make those doubles It's never going to be robotic."

articles.title: Luke Littler insists 'clean sweep very much on' as he attends Warrington mural unveiling days after World Matchplay win
articles.summary: Luke Littler attends unveiling of mural he "didn't want to see" in Warrington just four days on from storming to World Matchplay victory; 'The Nuke' has his sights set on unprecedented clean sweep amid stunning form
articles.body:
The 2026 PDC World Championship winner was frightenedly good in Blackpool, beating darts legend Phil Taylor's Matchplay record average of 106.31 with 111.04.

"I'm feeling very good," Littler told Sky Sports at the unveiling of his mural in Warrington on Thursday. "With performances like that, not many can stop me. Obviously, a tournament average of 111 was really, really good."

The 19-year-old has won every PDC title in 2026 so far - the World Championship, World Masters, UK Open, Premier League, World Cup and now the World Matchplay.

As it stands, he could still achieve an unprecedented clean sweep of eight ranking titles in the calendar - and Littler admitted that record is on his mind going forward, starting with working on qualifying to defend his Players Championship Finals title.

"The clean sweep is very much on," he said. "I think you can only look at what's coming up. For myself now, I can't go and say 'I'm going to win the World Championships'. That's in another five or six months.

"You've just got to look at what's in front of you. I've got a nice two-week holiday to Orlando tomorrow as well to look forward to. I think the clean sweep, it's very much on.

"As long as I qualify for Minehead, whether I win the World Series, the European, it's all coming up. It's a busy end of the year, but we'll see."

If a clean sweep was achieved, where does Littler think it would rank in terms of sporting achievement?

"For darts, I think it would be up there with probably one of the best," he said. "No one's ever done it. That's what I'm going for. I like to break all these records."

Littler's mural was unveiled in his hometown Warrington just four days on from breezing past Gerwyn Price to win yet another title in Blackpool.

The teen darts sensation signed his name on the artwork, took time to pose with fans for photos and played darts in front of the crowd present.

However he is still keeping himself grounded, both mentally and physically.

"[The mural is] very good," Littler said. "I actually saw it yesterday or the day before. I didn't want to see it, but they've done a really good job.

"I'm really happy. Someone said you can see it from miles away. It's that big, it's that tall.

"At first, they wanted me to sit on the roof. I said no chance! I'll just stand on the pavement."

Littler's next match will come in Leicester on the Pro Tour on August 25 and 26 at Players Championship 27 and 28 as he looks to secure his place at the Players Championship Finals in Minehead.

articles.title: Liverpool: Key questions answered as Amit Bhatia, Jeff Bezos and Eduardo Saverin agree purchase of strategic minority stake
articles.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos is part of the Amit Bhatia-led consortium that has agreed to buy a stake in Liverpool; Sky News reports the group are buying around one third of the Reds in a deal valuing the club at more than $7bn (£5.2bn); we take a deep dive into what the deal could mean
articles.body:
The world's third richest person is part of the group fronted by former QPR co-owner Amit Bhatia. Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is also part of the syndicate.

According to Sky News , the consortium has agreed to buy a roughly one-third stake in the club in a deal that values Liverpool at more than $7bn (£5.2bn). Closing of the transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.

We take a look at some of the key questions surrounding what the deal could look like...

The Bezos-backed consortium bought a 38 per cent stake in Liverpool from FSG.

It was initially suggested by sources close to the deal that the investment was for 30-33 per cent of the Premier League club.

However, Sky Sports News can confirm that 1892 Holdings has bought a stake closer to 40 per cent in Liverpool.

Sky Sports News reported last week that Liverpool's new minority investors have an option to become majority shareholders of the Premier League club.

According to Sky's US partner CNBC, this option is active for 12 months and would value Liverpool at around $8bn.

Sources have stressed the existence of such an agreement is not a guarantee of any future transaction.

Liverpool's statement last week said FSG continues to retain majority ownership and operational control of the club.

Bezos is one of the most famous businessmen in the world and the owner of e-commerce giant Amazon, which he founded in 1994 out of his Seattle garage.

His other investments include aerospace company Blue Origin and venture capital firm Nash Holdings, which is the ownership vehicle for The Washington Post.

Bhatia is a 46-year-old British Indian entrepreneur, who has an investment banking background.

He currently manages a multi-asset investment firm called AyBe Capital which invests in range of diversified sectors including technology, media, property and real estate, consumer retail and health.

Bhatia is married to Vanisha Mittal Bhatia, who is the daughter of Indian billionaire Lakshmi Mittal.

He leads and manages 1892 Holdings, the consortium that has agreed the minority investment in Liverpool with majority owners Fenway Sports Group.

Forbes estimates that Bezos' personal fortune is in the region of $281bn (£209bn), making him the third-richest person in the world behind Elon Musk and Google co-founder Larry Page.

It's unclear how much Bhatia himself is worth. But his father-in-law, billionaire steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, is worth an estimated £23.2bn according to Forbes. That makes him the 72nd richest person in the world.

Bezos is a big American Football fan and has previously been reported to have explored bids for the Washington Commanders and the Seattle Seahawks.

He is not known to hold a significant stake in any other sports team or enterprise currently.

Bhatia was just 28 when he joined the board of directors and became vice-chairman of QPR in 2007 after the Mittal family bought a 20 per cent stake in QPR, joining Bernie Ecclestone and Flavio Briatore as investors in the London club.

He spent five years as QPR chairman between 2018 and 2023 and stayed on as a director and co-owner until earlier this week when he transferred his stake in the club to majority owner Ruben Gnanalingam.

Through AyBe capital, Bhatia is an investor in TGL - Rory McIlroy and Tiger Woods' golf league which fuses golf and technology and features six teams with some of the best players in the world in a season-long competition.

His firm also invests in Switch Hitter, which is a media brand founded by Kevin Pietersen, delivering exclusive interviews and content with the world's top cricketers.

Earlier this year, Bhatia's father-in-law acquired a 75 per cent stake in the Rajasthan Royals Indian Premier League cricket franchise.

FSG were under no pressure to sell but did indicate in 2022 that they were open to new investment in Liverpool, with the sale of a small stake to Dynasty Equity completed the following year.

Liverpool have enjoyed huge success under FSG, lifting every major trophy available to win.

FSG may think it is mission accomplished somewhat as far they are concerned, and therefore were amenable to fresh investment. They also stand to make a huge profit on their initial investment, with the deal for a 30 per cent stake worth more than five times what they paid for the entire club back in 2010.

Could the Bezos-backed group take over Liverpool?

Liverpool's new minority investors have an option to become majority shareholders of the Premier League club for a valuation of around $8bn in the next 12 months, according to Sky's US partner CNBC.

Sky Sports News has been told the agreement announced today includes a framework for future investment from the Jeff Bezos-backed consortium.

However, sources have stressed that the existence of such an agreement is not a guarantee of any future transaction.

Liverpool's statement says FSG continues to retain majority ownership and operational control of the club.

Liverpool are the fourth most valuable club in the world. The consortium's investment in Liverpool values the club somewhere in the region of £5.2bn ($7bn), making it one of the sport's richest-ever deals.

FSG have complete operational control of Liverpool, but private equity firms RedBird Capital and Arctos Sports Partners hold minority stakes in the club. Dynasty Equity are also passive investors in Liverpool after injecting £164m into the club in 2023 in a deal valuing Liverpool at more than $4.5bn.

FSG were known as New England Sports Ventures when they paid £300m for Liverpool in October 2010 after a tumultuous period under former owners Tom Hicks and George Gillett.

The deal - which was first reported on at the end of last month - has accelerated at a rapid pace. Now that everything has been agreed, the closing of the transaction will happen after regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions are met.

Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin and his wife Elaine are also part of the syndicate of investors. Saverin, 44, was part of a consortium which assembled an unsuccessful takeover bid for Chelsea during the 2022 auction triggered by Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Summer transfer spending: Premier League, EFL, WSL, Scottish Premiership, LaLiga, Ligue 1, Serie A and Bundesliga breakdowns
articles.summary: From England's top four divisions to LaLiga, Serie A, Bundesliga, Ligue 1, Scottish Premiership and Women’s Super League - we break down how much clubs spent in the 2026 summer transfer market across the continent
articles.body:
Premier League clubs have smashed the transfer spending record after splashing £3.56bn on new signings.

The previous record of £3.19bn, set last summer, was surpassed following another extraordinary window across the top flight.

Clubs also recouped £2.25bn from player sales, contributing to a combined net spend of £1.30bn.

Premier League spending has now exceeded £2bn in each of the last five summer windows, with expenditure accelerating dramatically since 2022/23.

This summer's record outlay is almost three times the amount clubs spent a decade ago, when the 2016/17 total stood at £1.19bn.

The record has been broken despite Premier League clubs also generating another huge sum through sales, underlining the remarkable volume of money moving through the division.

Manchester City spent a league-high £440.3m during the window, followed by Chelsea (£342.4m), Spurs (£334m) and Newcastle (£275.2m).

In terms of net spend, Liverpool topped the table with £219.4m, followed by Ipswich (£190.7m), Spurs (£176m) and Hull (£160.5m).

At the other end of the scale, Chelsea finished the window £67.3m in profit after generating £409.7m from player sales.

Manchester City signed Enzo Fernandez from Chelsea for a joint-Premier League record £125m, matching Alexander Isak's move from Newcastle to Liverpool last summer.

Bradley Barcola (£123m) and Morgan Rogers ( £117m) were also among the window's biggest moves, while Elliot Anderson joined Manchester City for £116m and Sandro Tonali joined Spurs for £100m.

The scale of the market was reflected at the very top end: 20 players moved to Premier League clubs for fees of £50m or more.

Premier League clubs were also active sellers, with several of the summer's biggest transfers involving players moving either between English clubs or overseas.

Hull were the busiest recruiters, completing 17 permanent signings, followed by Ipswich (16), Chelsea (14), Brighton (13) and Coventry (12).

Meanwhile, Brighton , Aston Villa and Crystal Palace shipped a league-high 24 players out on permanent deals, ahead of Ipswich (22).

Championship clubs also set a new summer spending record, with expenditure reaching £301.3m.

That comfortably eclipsed the previous high of £204.2m, set last summer.

However, clubs recouped £506.4m from player sales, meaning the division collectively registered a transfer profit of £205.1m.

Wrexham , Stoke , and Norwich recorded the highest net spends in the division, while West Ham , Burnley and Southampton generated the biggest transfer profits.

The promoted and relegated clubs helped drive some of the largest numbers.

But the division continues to be an important seller of talent: Championship clubs have collectively generated a transfer profit every summer since 2016/17.

You can use the interactive tables below to find every signing and outgoing involving League One clubs this summer.

You can use the interactive tables below to find every signing and outgoing involving League Two clubs this summer.

Premier League clubs have again comfortably outspent their counterparts across Europe's other major domestic leagues.

Serie A clubs spent £846.2m , followed by LaLiga (£615.1m), Bundesliga (£507.6m) and Ligue 1 (£496.2m).

But the picture changes significantly when sales are factored in.

Serie A recorded the highest net spend at £255.3m, while Ligue 1 clubs collectively generated a transfer profit of £600.8m after recouping £1.1bn from player sales.

The contrast with the Premier League is considerable: English top-flight clubs have spent around four times as much as Serie A this summer.

However, Europe's major leagues remain a crucial source of Premier League recruitment, while substantial fees have also flowed in the opposite direction.

Real Madrid have the highest net spend outside the Premier League at £143.8m, followed by Juventus (£118.2m) and Fiorentina (£104.6m).

Yan Diomande is the most expensive signing across Europe's other leading leagues, completing a £107.1m move from RB Leipzig to Real Madrid ( Sky Sports fee: £120m ).

It sums up a wild Transfer Deadline Day that the British transfer record was matched in the final hours of the window. Enzo Fernandez's move from Chelsea to Manchester City completed an extraordinary summer in which spending went stratospheric.

Sky Sports' Adam Bate looks at how it unfolded and where it leaves Premier League clubs and supporters with the window now shut - but everyone still wanting more...

articles.title: Why Folarin Balogun's Everton move collapsed on Deadline Day leaving Toffees, Chelsea and Monaco frustrated
articles.summary: Sky Sports News takes you inside why Folarin Balogun's move to Everton collapsed on Deadline Day to leave the Toffees, Chelsea and Monaco upset; before Balogun's decision, Monaco had pulled the plug on a deal for midfielder Lamine Camara to join Chelsea as their Enzo Fernandez replacement
articles.body:
Chelsea , Everton and Monaco ended up very frustrated as Folarin Balogun opted against joining Everton at the last minute after Monaco had earlier pulled out of a deal to sell Lamine Camara to Chelsea, who wanted the midfielder as their Enzo Fernandez replacement.

The two Premier League sides were particularly left fuming about the situation.

Here, Sky Sports News takes you inside why both deals collapsed on a dramatic end to Deadline Day…

Monaco needed to make a sale to help resolve a debt issue, while Everton needed a striker.

Balogun became a solution for both parties, and a £40m agreement was reached - but then came the first issue with the deal.

There was a problem with the USA international's medical after Everton found evidence of an injury, which Monaco and the player refuted, claiming he was fit to play immediately.

With the 11pm deadline approaching, Everton decided to proceed with the transfer but attempted to renegotiate the deal on cheaper terms in case the injury left him unable to play.

The club-to-club deal became much more performance-related, with clauses inserted that meant Monaco would get less money if Balogun could not play.

Crucially, it is understood nothing changed with Balogun's personal terms.

How Everton's Zirkzee move angers Balogun

Amid a renegotiation of the Balogun deal, Chelsea reached an agreement with Monaco to sign midfielder Camara as a replacement for Fernandez, who was set to join Manchester City in a joint-British record £125m deal.

Meanwhile, Everton made a loan offer for Manchester United forward Joshua Zirkzee , which was rejected.

Sky Sports News understands Everton offered to pay a total fee of around £10m for Zirkzee, which included his wages for the season and a loan fee.

But the feeling at Old Trafford was that Everton's approach came too late and was not of value.

The Toffees' pursuit of Zirkzee is what upset Balogun, who felt the club were going behind his back to sign someone else.

Balogun's unhappiness with Everton was revealed by Monaco chief Thiago Scuro at a press conference on Wednesday.

He said: "Balogun's allegation is that I'm not feeling well because of the way the club treated me.

"I'm not feeling well because Everton's medical department brought doubts about my future or my health.

"I have nothing (no medical problem), so I'm not comfortable to sign a long contract here."

Everton are understood to be surprised at the allegation that Balogun was made to feel unwanted, given they never renegotiated his personal terms and clearly wanted to get the deal done.

The renegotiation of the guaranteed fee payable to Monaco justified the risk given the issue with the medical.

Sky Sports News also understands that Everton's interest in Zirkzee was separate from the Balogun deal, with the club prepared to sign both players.

Everton feel the ex-Arsenal forward misunderstood their Zirkzee approach - they were not turning their attention to a different player.

Believing Balogun would be joining Everton, Monaco pulled the plug on Chelsea's deal for Camara.

The Ligue 1 side preferred selling Balogun over Camara because they only needed the money from one player sale.

But Balogun then sensationally decided to walk away from his Everton move over what he perceived as poor treatment from the Merseysiders.

His dramatic decision, which saw him miss out on his dream Premier League move, meant all three clubs were left disappointed.

Monaco kept both Balogun and Camara, failing to raise the money they wanted.

Everton missed out on signing a striker, leaving them with just one recognised striker, Thierno Barry , in their squad after selling Beto to Fiorentina in a £15.4m Deadline Day deal.

And Chelsea were left with no Fernandez replacement after he joined Man City - a deal which the Blues could have pulled out of but honoured despite having no replacement.

The question now is whether these deals could be revived in January? Well, you would say it is unlikely after this shambles.

articles.title: Man Utd miss attacking spark against Everton as Ezri Konsa for Arsenal - Premier League hits and misses
articles.summary: The Sky Sports football writers analyse Sunday's Premier League action as Man Utd lack a killer touch against Everton, Ezri Konsa impresses on his first Arsenal start, and Morgan Rogers has a mixed afternoon against the club that tried to sign him
articles.body:
Michael Carrick responded to a question about Manchester United's disappointing start to the season in a relaxed manner. "It's not that bad," he insisted, smiling at the assessment after only three gamed played. He's right to point out how early it is in the campaign.

But what he can't defend is how poorly his side have imposed themselves on two newly promoted teams and Everton. For just the second time in the last 50 years, Man Utd have conceded two goals in each of their first three outings.

None of those opponents - Hull, Ipswich or Everton - are expected to be prolific scorers this term. Carrick's side will face much sterner tests. They play the Manchester derby next weekend, in fact. And have issues at both ends to address before they do.

The spark is missing. Carrick put his head down in sheer disbelief after his side were twice pegged back by worldie strikes at the Hill Dickinson, but the question that needs answering is why Everton were invited back in in the first place. United were the more creative side but often ran out of gas by the final third.

Everton's xG value was greater by the close and they managed double the amount of shots on target (six). The hosts covered more distance and completed more sprints, too.

For all United's control, they lack proper punch and will need to encourage more consistency of output from their expensively-assembled forward line to make up for what they lack defensively. Laura Hunter

Arsenal had given the ball away and Chelsea were breaking through Morgan Rogers down the left.

But soon the Emirates went from anguish to raucous applause as Ezri Konsa came in with a hammer challenge. "A very English tackle," Mikel Arteta said after the game. "You guys love that more than a goal sometimes."

It was the battle between the Aston Villa player Arsenal were going to buy and the Villa player they ended up getting. But after Rogers gave Arsenal a fright after 77 seconds, it was Konsa's time to respond - and he came out on top overall.

It was a moment that announced the £55m signing in front of his new team. It demonstrated the reason why Arsenal went for him, when so many clamoured for more signings further forward.

It also summed up an excellent first start for Arsenal, as Konsa topped a lot of metrics despite playing just 20 minutes of competitive football since the World Cup ended before this Chelsea game.

"I hear they like clean sheets here," Konsa said. He understands the Arsenal assignment. No clean sheet on start No 1 - but he is part of a phenomenal group of Gunners defenders. Sam Blitz

Chelsea's visit to the Emirates Stadium could not have started any better for Rogers. Having spurned the Gunners before choosing Chelsea, he relished his superbly-taken opener after 77 seconds, gesturing towards the badge as he celebrated.

He continued to play with a swagger in the first period, effortlessly pinging a cross-field pass to the feet of Pedro Neto on one occasion and almost adding a second goal when he curled narrowly wide following one of several dangerous forays into the box.

The second half was more difficult. The Arsenal fans loved the crunching tackle from Konsa that left him on the turf and his frustration boiled over when he confronted Declan Rice following an off-the-ball trip during another Chelsea attack.

He wasn't the only Chelsea player whose focus appeared to waver. His goal, added to the one he scored against Fulham, continues a strong start to the season. But he will have to wait for Arsenal's return to Stamford Bridge for a chance to have the final say. Nick Wright

Maybe Everton did have a good Deadline Day after all.

Jack Grealish and Ainsley Maitland-Niles were brought in late, but both made a telling impact as Everton fought back for a 2-2 draw with Manchester United.

Grealish, in particular, provided something Everton had badly lacked. The winger kept driving at United, forcing them backwards. He drew a booking from Diogo Dalot, created two chances and, most importantly, injected some life into an Everton attack that had looked short of inspiration.

There was a swagger to his performance, too. Every time Grealish got the ball, there was a feeling something might happen. Everton finally had a player willing to take responsibility and run at United rather than simply recycle possession.

Then came Maitland-Niles' Hollywood moment.

The new signing popped up with the equaliser to cap a memorable first appearance and rescue a point for David Moyes' side.

Perhaps the business done on Deadline Day was actually masterstroke. Lewis Jones

articles.title: Luke Humphries says opening up about his mental health helped him rise to the top of darts
articles.summary: Luke Humphries has been hailed for opening up about his mental health issues; the world No 2 believes speaking about his struggles has helped him rise to the top of darts
articles.body:
Humphries, who has partnered with the Samaritans to mark World Suicide Prevention Day, was on the grind of the PDC Tour when he suffered an anxiety attack midway through a tournament in 2019 and considered quitting.

He spoke openly about his troubles, and it had a positive impact on him as he surged to the top of the game, culminating in winning the 2024 World Championship title and becoming world No 1.

"For me, the best thing I ever did was go and see a doctor and go and tell him my feelings," Humphries said in conversation with a Samaritans volunteer.

"Look who I am now. I've achieved so much from doing that and I'm so glad I did.

"The first step is to be open and honest about it. When I told my mum and dad stuff, they were really helpful. They helped me get where I needed to be.

"With what I was going through, the way I was feeling and where I thought my career was going to go, to end up with nine major titles, and a World Championship and a World Cup and a Matchplay four or five years later, I would never have thought that was going to happen to me.

"I thought that would have been impossible because of the way I was feeling at the time.

"I just felt like my career was going to end and I almost thought about giving it up because the stress was playing on me a lot.

"I decided to stick with it and it was the best choice I ever made, to be honest. It really did pay its dividends."

The Samaritans say one in four people experience suicidal thoughts, with suicide being the biggest killer of men under 50.

Humphries, who will play in next week's World Series of Darts Finals, revealed he still suffers from anxiety but knows how to handle it.

"I still get those moments of anxiety and stuff, but they're just random," he said.

"They're not in moments you would expect, surrounded by hundreds of people. It could just be a random moment when I'm driving in the car by myself and you just get this bout of anxiety.

"It's strange, but I know how to deal with it better. You don't spiral, I think that's the most important thing. That's why I feel my mental health has been so much better in the last three to four years."

Humphries hailed for 'creating different kind of legacy'

Simon Gunning, chief executive officer of Campaign Against Living Miserably (CALM), hailed Humphries after the world No 2 opened up about his mental health struggles on World Suicide Prevention Day.

He said: "It's hard to overstate the impact these stories have.

"We know from people calling our helpline that someone like Luke sharing their experience can be the turning point they need to seek help.

"What Luke has achieved on the board is extraordinary, but his willingness to speak openly about his mental health is creating a different kind of legacy.

"He's giving people permission to open up when they're struggling, and that ripple effect is profound."

If you have been affected by any of these issues or are worried about someone else, visit Sky Sports' Support for our Viewers page for more information on how to receive support.

You can also contact Samaritans free of charge, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, by calling 116 123 or visiting .
